reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A genetically heterogeneous group of dominantly inherited progressive ataxias, numbered by locus (for example SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, SCA6, SCA7)
Many of the common subtypes are caused by expanded CAG trinucleotide repeats encoding polyglutamine tracts, and repeat length often correlates inversely with age at onset
Anticipation, with earlier onset and greater severity in successive generations, is a feature of the repeat-expansion subtypes
Core features are progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, and abnormal eye movements, with additional signs varying by subtype
SCA3 (Machado-Joseph disease) is among the most common worldwide and can include parkinsonism, neuropathy, and prominent eye-movement abnormalities
SCA7 is distinctive for associated pigmentary retinopathy and progressive visual loss, and SCA6 tends to be a relatively pure, later-onset cerebellar syndrome
Diagnosis combines family history, clinical phenotype, and targeted or panel genetic testing for repeat expansions and other mutations
Management is largely supportive, addressing gait safety, speech and swallowing, and associated features, since disease-modifying therapy is limited
reference.pathophysiology: The spinocerebellar ataxias comprise many distinct genetic disorders that share progressive degeneration of the cerebellum and its connections, often extending to the brainstem, spinal cord, and other structures. In the common polyglutamine subtypes, expanded CAG repeats produce abnormal proteins that misfold, aggregate, and cause neuronal dysfunction and loss, with a threshold repeat length determining disease and longer expansions producing earlier, more severe disease. Other subtypes arise from noncoding repeat expansions or conventional mutations affecting ion channels or other neuronal proteins, giving overlapping but distinguishable phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive ataxias including Friedreich ataxia
Acquired cerebellar ataxias (alcohol, paraneoplastic, immune-mediated, toxic)
additionalInvestigations: Targeted or panel genetic testing for repeat expansions and point mutations
Brain MRI to assess cerebellar and brainstem atrophy
Detailed family history and pedigree analysis
Ophthalmological review where retinopathy is suspected (as in SCA7)
Nerve conduction studies when peripheral neuropathy features are present
Exclusion of acquired and treatable causes of ataxia
redFlags: Rapid progression raising concern for an acquired or paraneoplastic cause rather than a hereditary ataxia
Falls with injury from worsening gait ataxia
Visual loss suggesting retinal involvement in relevant subtypes
reference.prognosis: Most subtypes are slowly progressive over years to decades with gradual loss of independent mobility and speech; life expectancy is often reduced in more severe subtypes, largely through complications such as aspiration, while relatively pure subtypes may follow a more benign course.
pitfalls: Assuming all cerebellar ataxia is hereditary and overlooking treatable acquired causes
Not recognising anticipation and the significance of family history across generations
Missing subtype-specific features such as retinopathy in SCA7
Ordering untargeted testing without a clinical and pedigree-guided strategy
management: Provide symptomatic and supportive care coordinated through a specialist ataxia service, as no disease-modifying therapy exists
Maximise function and safety with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, balance and gait training, and mobility aids to reduce falls
Offer speech and language therapy for dysarthria and swallow assessment with diet modification or gastrostomy where aspiration risk develops
Treat associated features symptomatically, including spasticity, tremor, parkinsonism, neuropathic pain and depression
Manage subtype-specific complications such as retinal surveillance in SCA7 and seizure control where relevant
Monitor progression with standardised ataxia rating scales and surveil for aspiration and respiratory complications
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, discussing anticipation and predictive or cascade testing
